messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
parts:
For a start, I'd use a scale parameterization rather than
a sqrt(precision) one. And include priors.

You want to vectorize those sampling statements (which
means converting the arrays of vectors to matrices --- indexing
with one index still provides a row vector).

You want to remove the unused definition of I.

And you want to move r_new to be defined in generated quantities
using normal_rng:

generated quantities {
real<lower=0, upper=5> r_new[D_new]; //pridict rating
for (d in 1:D_New)
r_new[d] <- normal_rng(...);
}

But that won't quite work, because there's no guarantee the
result is in (0, 5). You probably want to do this all on
the log-odds scale (logit link).

Then, when everything's fixed, try fitting simulated data
at a reasonable scale where you know the answer to make sure
you're getting the right answers.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
parts:
> On Feb 14, 2016, at 10:07 AM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> @Bob, tons of thanks for your patience and answer. Your explanation is quite clear but I am just a little bit confused of something, as I am quite newbie to stan. Do you mean change the
> for (d in 1:D){
> r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha);
> }
> to
> for (d in 1:D){
> r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha^2);
> }
> by "use a scale parameterization rather than a sqrt(precision) one" and add a prior distribution over alpha?

Stan parameterizes the normal using standard deviation.
Most ath notation uses variance, which is std-dev^2.
BUGS uses precision, which is 1 / variance.

I just meant that if you were parameterizing in terms of alpha
and then using normal(..., 1 / alpha), then alpha is the sqrt
of the precision. I suggested just making sigma a std
deviation and using normal(..., sigma) as in all the examples
in our manual.

BUGS tended use gamma priors for precision or inverse gammas
for variance because of conjugacy --- Stan doesn't require conjugacy
for efficiency.
> And is there any example of limiting the value in a certain range in the stan manual? Thank you so much.

If there is for anything other than a probability, it's
probably a mistake. We're trying to discourage interval
bounds for anything other than physical/conceptual constraints.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
parts:
There's an ordinal logit model that produces rankings
based on an underlying logistic parameterization.

Or you can take a prediction and just apply

f(x) = 5 * inv_logit(x)

which maps x in (-inf, inf) to (0, 5).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
parts:
The second parameter of the normal is a scale parameter
and the std-dev of a normal is the scale. You don't want
to be squaring that variable --- it's not a variance parameter.

You probably do want to provide some kind of prior, but probably
not one that keeps it away from zero.

You want to figure out which normal is causing your problem and
ask whether 0 is consistent as an SD. I'm not sure the hierarchical
priors are buying you much for the factors.

Also, just a fair warning: factor models are very hard to fit.

I'm appending a working example with some simulation code, and you see
that the autocorrelations in the fits are huge, so it'd require a lot
of samples to fit well.

- Bob

data {
int<lower=0> I;
int<lower=0> J;

int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1, upper=I> ii[N];
int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N];
real y[N];

int<lower=0> K;
}
parameters {
row_vector[K] alpha[I];
vector[K] beta[J];
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
sigma ~ normal(0, 1);
for (i in 1:I) alpha[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
for (j in 1:J) beta[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(alpha[ii[n]] * beta[jj[n]], sigma);
}

===========================

library(rstan);
I <- 200;
J <- 100;
K <- 3;
N <- 10000;

alpha <- matrix(rnorm(I * K), I, K);
beta <- matrix(rnorm(J * K), J, K);
sigma <- 0.75;
ii <- sample(1:I, N, replace=TRUE);
jj <- sample(1:J, N, replace=TRUE);
y <- rep(NA, N);
for (n in 1:N) {
y[n] <- rnorm(1, t(alpha[ii[n],]) %*% beta[jj[n],], sigma);
}

fit <- stan("pmf.stan", data=c("I", "J", "K", "N", "ii", "jj", "y"),
chains=1, iter=5000, refresh=50);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
parts:
Also, start with simpler models. Take the scales to be fixed,
fit that, and later work out the generalization to a hierarchical
model. Then you can see step by step what is causing problems
with fitting.

- Bob

> On Feb 15, 2016, at 1:05 PM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob, thank you so, so much for that. To keep it far away from zero, I set all the alpha with lower bound of 0.001:

> r[d] ~ normal(u[jj[d]] * i[ii[d]], alpha);
> Seems no error like last time generates any more, but it stops at "Chain 0, Iteration: 1 / 1000 [ 0%] (Warmup)" for a long time till now.
>
> I also tried to give a prior distribution over alpha but the error message generates again.
>
> I wonder whether the trick in your code is put the y[n] again outside the stan code? But why does it work?
>
> Thanks a lot.
>
>
> 在 2016年2月16日星期二 UTC+8上午12:45:14，Bob Carpenter写道：
> The second parameter of the normal is a scale parameter
> and the std-dev of a normal is the scale. You don't want
> to be squaring that variable --- it's not a variance parameter.
>
> You probably do want to provide some kind of prior, but probably
> not one that keeps it away from zero.
>
> You want to figure out which normal is causing your problem and
> ask whether 0 is consistent as an SD. I'm not sure the hierarchical
> priors are buying you much for the factors.
>
> Also, just a fair warning: factor models are very hard to fit.
>
> I'm appending a working example with some simulation code, and you see
> that the autocorrelations in the fits are huge, so it'd require a lot
> of samples to fit well.
>
> - Bob
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> I;
> int<lower=0> J;
>
> int<lower=0> N;
> int<lower=1, upper=I> ii[N];
> int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N];
> real y[N];
>
> int<lower=0> K;
> }
> parameters {
> row_vector[K] alpha[I];
> vector[K] beta[J];
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> model {
> sigma ~ normal(0, 1);
> for (i in 1:I) alpha[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
> for (j in 1:J) beta[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
> for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(alpha[ii[n]] * beta[jj[n]], sigma);
> }
>
> ===========================
>
> library(rstan);
> I <- 200;
> J <- 100;
> K <- 3;
> N <- 10000;
>
> alpha <- matrix(rnorm(I * K), I, K);
> beta <- matrix(rnorm(J * K), J, K);
> sigma <- 0.75;
> ii <- sample(1:I, N, replace=TRUE);
> jj <- sample(1:J, N, replace=TRUE);
> y <- rep(NA, N);
> for (n in 1:N) {
> y[n] <- rnorm(1, t(alpha[ii[n],]) %*% beta[jj[n],], sigma);
> }
>
> fit <- stan("pmf.stan", data=c("I", "J", "K", "N", "ii", "jj", "y"),
> chains=1, iter=5000, refresh=50);
>
>
> > On Feb 15, 2016, at 11:39 AM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Daniel, but why the normal_rng doesn't support (real,vector) but just (real, real). And I also see a lot of examples using scale parameter as deviation. But they don't get the error like me. So maybe there is another problem?
> >
> > 在 2016年2月15日星期一 UTC+8下午10:05:59，Daniel Lee写道：
> > The scale parameter is the last parameter in the normal distribution.
> >
> > On Feb 15, 2016, at 8:06 AM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >>
> >>
> >> 在 2016年2月15日星期一 UTC+8下午9:04:35，Zichao Li写道：
> >>
> >> I have tried what you said, but it still does not work. The stan code I have tried are attached. Both of the versions got the error:
> >> Exception thrown at line 40: stan::math::normal_log: Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0!
> >>
> >> They are pointing the same line of code:
> >> r[d] ~ normal(u[jj[d]] * i[ii[d]]', sigma);
> >> or
> >> r[d] ~ normal(u[jj[d]] * i[ii[d]]', alpha);
> >>
> >
> > I don't see how those are the same lines of code.
> >
> > Make sure sigma is defined as real<lower = 0>. And the same with sigma.
> >
> >
> >
> >> Do you have any idea
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> 在 2016年2月15日星期一 UTC+8下午3:49:14，Bob Carpenter写道：
> >> There's an ordinal logit model that produces rankings
> >> based on an underlying logistic parameterization.
> >>
> >> Or you can take a prediction and just apply
> >>
> >> f(x) = 5 * inv_logit(x)
> >>
> >> which maps x in (-inf, inf) to (0, 5).
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>
> >> > On Feb 14, 2016, at 10:45 PM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >
> >> > As you said,
> >> > But that won't quite work, because there's no guarantee the
> >> > result is in (0, 5). You probably want to do this all on
> >> > the log-odds scale (logit link).
> >> > I wonder if there is any example of it in the user manual?
> >> >
> >> > Thanks,
> >> > Rylan
> >> > 在 2016年2月15日星期一 UTC+8上午2:31:13，Bob Carpenter写道：
> >> >
> >> > > On Feb 14, 2016, at 10:07 AM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> > >
> >> > > @Bob, tons of thanks for your patience and answer. Your explanation is quite clear but I am just a little bit confused of something, as I am quite newbie to stan. Do you mean change the
> >> > > for (d in 1:D){
> >> > > r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha);
> >> > > }
> >> > > to
> >> > > for (d in 1:D){
> >> > > r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha^2);
> >> > > }
> >> > > by "use a scale parameterization rather than a sqrt(precision) one" and add a prior distribution over alpha?
> >> >
> >> > Stan parameterizes the normal using standard deviation.
> >> > Most ath notation uses variance, which is std-dev^2.
> >> > BUGS uses precision, which is 1 / variance.
> >> >
> >> > I just meant that if you were parameterizing in terms of alpha
> >> > and then using normal(..., 1 / alpha), then alpha is the sqrt
> >> > of the precision. I suggested just making sigma a std
> >> > deviation and using normal(..., sigma) as in all the examples
> >> > in our manual.
> >> >
> >> > BUGS tended use gamma priors for precision or inverse gammas
> >> > for variance because of conjugacy --- Stan doesn't require conjugacy
> >> > for efficiency.
> >> >
> >> > > And is there any example of limiting the value in a certain range in the stan manual? Thank you so much.
> >> >
> >> > If there is for anything other than a probability, it's
> >> > probably a mistake. We're trying to discourage interval
> >> > bounds for anything other than physical/conceptual constraints.
> >> >
> >> > - Bob
